subject: Agriculture
title: Desalination for Farming
description: A micro-lesson that makes Desalination for Farming usable.

hook.text: 97% of Earth's water is salty. If we could affordably desalinate seawater, every coastal desert could become a farm.

buildup.text: Reverse osmosis pushes seawater through membranes to remove salt. It works but requires enormous energy.

discovery.text: Israel desalinates 80% of its drinking water and recycles 87% of wastewater for agriculture—the world's highest rate.

twist.text: Desalination costs have dropped 80% since the 1990s. At solar-powered scale, it could become affordable for irrigation.

climax.text: The Sahara Forest Project combines solar, desalination, and greenhouses to grow food in Jordan's desert.

punchline.text: Unlimited saltwater, unlimited sunlight. The desert just needs desalination.

quiz.question: How much of Israel's wastewater is recycled for agriculture?

details.summary: Desalination for farming converts seawater or brackish water into freshwater suitable for irrigation. This topic covers reverse osmosis technology, energy costs, brine management, and where desalinated water is already supporting agriculture in arid regions.
details.whyItMatters: Freshwater scarcity threatens agriculture in many coastal and arid regions. Desalination offers a climate-independent water source, though high energy costs and brine disposal remain challenges.
takeaways: Reverse osmosis is the dominant desalination technology, using membrane filtration
Israel irrigates a significant share of its crops with desalinated Mediterranean water
Energy costs make desalinated water 3–5 times more expensive than groundwater

faq.question: How does desalination work for agricultural use?
faq.answer: Seawater or brackish water is forced through semi-permeable membranes using high pressure in a process called reverse osmosis. Salt and impurities are removed, producing freshwater clean enough for irrigation of crops.

faq.question: Is desalinated water cost-effective for farming?
faq.answer: Currently, desalinated water costs $0.50–$1.50 per cubic meter, making it viable mainly for high-value crops or regions with no alternative water sources. Declining solar energy costs are gradually improving the economics.
